h: A Spring, a Priory and Roses With Pedigree
p: The name Mottisfont comes from the font, or spring, that still bubbles up in the grounds, and it's worth seeking out. The priory here was founded around the start of the thirteenth century for Augustinian canons, and after Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries it was handed to William Sandys, one of the king's courtiers, who turned the church into a house. Later owners kept remodelling, which is why the building is such a fascinating jumble of eras.

Those famous roses have a real pedigree too. The collection of old-fashioned shrub roses in the walled garden was gathered by the great plantsman Graham Stuart Thomas in the 1970s, and it holds the National Collection of pre-1900 roses. In peak season it gets busy, so arrive early, savour the scent while it's still calm, then head into the house when the crowds build.

The River Test, which runs alongside, is one of England's most famous chalk streams, known around the world for trout fishing, and its water is so clear you can watch fish drifting in the current. Look out for them from the riverside paths.

Allow around half a day. Train fans can use Mottisfont and Dunbridge station, a walk away across the valley. Afterwards, Romsey Abbey is a must for anyone who loves Norman architecture, and the Sir Harold Hillier Gardens near Ampfield make a smashing second stop for keen gardeners.
